questions.question_text: Repair times at a garage are strongly right-skewed, with mean $55$ minutes and standard deviation $30$ minutes. A random sample of $48$ repair times is taken. Which statement is correct?

options.text: $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal, because the sample is random and $n\ge 30$.
$\bar{X}$ is right-skewed, because the population is right-skewed.
options.why: Assumed the sampling distribution copies the shape of the population instead of becoming normal.

options.text: The $48$ individual repair times are approximately normal, because $n\ge 30$.
options.why: Claimed the population becomes normal in a large sample; the theorem is about the sample mean, not the data.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded, because the population is not normal.
options.why: Treated a non-normal population as blocking the theorem, but the theorem holds whatever the population's shape.

questions.solution_text:
The sample is random.
$n=48$, and $48\ge 30$.
The shape of the population does not matter.
$\bar{X}$ is approximately normal.

questions.question_text: A population of house prices is strongly right-skewed. A random sample of $10$ prices is taken. Which statement is correct?

options.text: No conclusion of approximate normality can be drawn, because $n=10$ is below $30$.
$\bar{X}$ is approximately normal, because the theorem holds for every sample size.
options.why: Dropped the large-sample condition; the theorem needs $n\ge 30$ unless the population is already normal.

options.text: $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal, because averaging $10$ values always removes skew.
options.why: Assumed any amount of averaging produces normality, which is not what the theorem states.

options.text: The $10$ prices are approximately normal, because they were chosen at random.
options.why: Claimed the population becomes normal once sampled randomly; randomness does not change the population's shape.

questions.solution_text:
The sample is random, but $n=10$, and $10<30$.
The population is not normal, so there is no small-sample result either.
The central limit theorem cannot be used here.

questions.question_text: A population has mean $\mu=64$ and standard deviation $\sigma=24$. Random samples of size $144$ are taken. Which is the approximate distribution of $\bar{X}$?

options.why: Used the population variance $\sigma^2=576$ without dividing by $n$.
Gave the standard deviation $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=2$ where the second entry must be the variance.
Used the population standard deviation $\sigma=24$ instead of the variance of $\bar{X}$.

questions.solution_text:
$n=144$, and $144\ge 30$, so the central limit theorem applies.
$E(\bar{X})=64$
$\text{Var}(\bar{X})=\dfrac{24^2}{144}$
$=\dfrac{576}{144}$
$=4$
$\bar{X}$ is approximately $N(64,4)$

questions.question_text: A random digit generator produces the digits $0$ to $9$, each equally likely, so the population is uniform. One hundred digits are generated and their mean is calculated. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The mean of the $100$ digits is approximately normal, but the $100$ digits themselves are not.
The $100$ digits are approximately normal, because $n\ge 30$.
options.why: Claimed the population becomes normal in a large sample; the digits stay uniform however many are generated.

options.text: Both the $100$ digits and their mean are approximately normal.
options.why: Applied the theorem to the data as well as to the mean, when it describes only the mean.

options.text: Neither is approximately normal, because the population is uniform.
options.why: Treated a uniform population as blocking the theorem, but the theorem holds whatever the population's shape.

questions.solution_text:
A large random sample of digits still shows all ten digits about equally often, so it stays uniform.
The central limit theorem describes the sample mean.
$n=100\ge 30$, so the mean of the $100$ digits is approximately normal while the digits are not.

questions.question_text: Random samples are taken from a population, and the sample size is increased from $40$ to $360$. The standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ is multiplied by which factor?

options.why: Divided by the sample-size ratio $9$ itself instead of by its square root.
Got the size of the change right but the direction wrong; a larger sample makes $\bar{X}$ less spread out.
Multiplied by the sample-size ratio, ignoring both the square root and the fact that the spread shrinks.

questions.solution_text:
The standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.
For $n=40$ it is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{40}}$.
For $n=360$ it is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{360}}$.
$\dfrac{\sqrt{40}}{\sqrt{360}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{40}{360}}$
$=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{9}}$
$=\dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.question_text: For random samples of size $256$ taken from a certain population, the central limit theorem gives $\bar{X}$ as approximately $N(310,4)$. What is the standard deviation of the population?

options.why: Gave the standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ itself, without multiplying by $\sqrt{n}$ to recover $\sigma$.
Gave the population variance $\sigma^2$ instead of the standard deviation $\sigma$.
Divided by $\sqrt{n}=16$ instead of multiplying by it, reversing the direction of the calculation.

questions.question_text: How must the sample size be changed so that the standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ becomes one fifth of its present value?

options.text: Multiply the sample size by $25$
Multiply the sample size by $5$
options.why: Used the factor itself rather than its square, forgetting that $n$ sits under a square root.

options.text: Divide the sample size by $5$
options.why: Reduced the sample size, which makes the standard deviation larger, not smaller.

options.text: Divide the sample size by $25$
options.why: Squared the factor correctly but reduced the sample size, so the spread increases instead.

questions.solution_text:
The standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.
Dividing it by $5$ needs $\sqrt{n}$ multiplied by $5$.
$(5\sqrt{n})^2=25n$
The sample size must be multiplied by $25$.

questions.question_text: A machine fills bags of flour. The weights are strongly right-skewed with mean $505$ g and standard deviation $18$ g. For which one of the following does the central limit theorem justify using a normal model?

options.text: The mean weight of a random sample of $36$ bags
The weight of one randomly chosen bag
options.why: Applied the theorem to a single observation; one weight comes straight from the right-skewed population.

options.text: The mean weight of a random sample of $4$ bags
options.why: Used a sample mean, but $n=4$ is far below the $n\ge 30$ needed for a non-normal population.

options.text: The weights of all bags produced in one day
options.why: Claimed the population becomes normal once enough bags are made; the population keeps its skew.

questions.solution_text:
The theorem describes a sample mean, so a single bag and the whole day's production are both ruled out.
Of the two sample means, $n=4$ is too small for a right-skewed population.
$n=36$, and $36\ge 30$, with a random sample.
A normal model is justified for the mean weight of a random sample of $36$ bags.
